title: Defection Detection: Measuring and Understanding the Predictive Accuracy of Customer Churn Models
harvard_reference: Neslin, S.A., Gupta, S., Kamakura, W., Lu, J. and Mason, C.H. (2006) 'Defection detection: measuring and understanding the predictive accuracy of customer churn models', Journal of Marketing Research, 43(2), pp. 204-211. doi:10.1509/jmkr.43.2.204.
abstract_summary: Descriptive meta-analysis of a churn-modelling tournament run by the Teradata Center for CRM at Duke University, in which 33 academics and practitioners submitted 44 entries built on an anonymous US wireless carrier's data (100,000-customer calibration set with 171 predictors; two validation sets of 51,306 and 100,462 customers, 1.8% churners). Entries were scored on top-decile lift and the Gini coefficient on both a current and a three-months-later validation set. Three findings: (1) methods matter - top-decile lift ranged from 1.07 to 3.01 and, via a profit model linking lift to campaign profitability, such differences are worth hundreds of thousands of dollars; (2) models have staying power, with negligible decay over three months; (3) a factor analysis of survey responses identified five modelling 'approaches' (logit, tree, practical, discriminant, explain) defined by estimation technique, variable-selection method and time allocation; logit and tree approaches performed best, discriminant and explain worst.

claims_supported.claim: Methodological choices (estimation technique, variable selection, time allocation) materially affect churn-model accuracy, and logistic regression and decision trees performed well in the churn tournament.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (p. 204): 'methods do matter' and approaches are 'characterized by variables such as estimation technique, variable selection procedure, number of variables included, and time allocated to steps in the model-building process'. Results, 'Regression Results of Performance' and Table 3 (pp. 207-208): 'Logit and tree approaches are positively associated with predictive performance ... both tend to do well' (logit factor coefficient .527, p = .001; tree .293, p = .042 on current lift), while discriminant and explain approaches carry consistently negative signs. Conclusions (p. 209): 'Logistic and tree approaches perform relatively well, the practical approach has average performance, and discriminant and explain approaches have the lowest performance', holding across both criteria and both validation sets. Implications (pp. 209-210): 'logit and tree approaches are good techniques with which to begin'. Caveat to state in the report: 'logit' and 'tree' are factor-analytic bundles that combine the technique with variable-selection and time-allocation habits, and the authors warn that 'the approaches mean more than just the statistical technique'; the winning entry used gradient tree boosting of small trees (p. 210), not a single decision tree.

claims_supported.claim: Top-decile lift and the Gini coefficient are appropriate business-facing metrics for churn models, and small accuracy differences can translate into large profit differences.
claims_supported.where: Tournament structure, 'Data' (p. 206): the two scoring criteria were top-decile lift and the Gini coefficient; 'Lift is probably the most commonly used prediction criterion in predictive modeling, and its relevance is demonstrated by the direct link between lift and profitability we demonstrated previously. The Gini coefficient represents the area between the cumulative lift curve and random prediction, so it is a broader measure than top-decile lift.' Overall Performance (p. 206): the criteria correlate above .9, so 'top-decile lift can be used by itself as a measure of predictive performance'. Equations 1-4 (p. 205) express campaign profit as a linear function of lift; 'Profit Impact of Results' (pp. 207-209): under the most conservative assumptions a one-unit change in lift is worth $1.71 per customer, a half-unit (one standard deviation) change $0.85 per customer, i.e. $427,500 for a firm with 5 million customers contacting 10%; the variation observed 'can easily amount to changes in profit in the hundreds of thousands of dollars by using one method rather than another'; Table 4 and p. 209 give $230,000 for a one-SD move toward the logit approach. Nuance: the paper's wording is 'managerially meaningful' rather than 'business-facing', and the accuracy gaps it monetises are one SD of lift (about 0.5) on a range it calls 'a wide spread'; 'small' is defensible only in the sense that a difference worth cents per customer becomes large at scale, so the report should phrase it that way.

caveats: The tournament data are a 2000s US wireless carrier's proprietary dataset (171 predictors, 1.8% monthly churn, oversampled to 50% churners for calibration), not the Kaggle IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, so results are transferable as methodological lessons rather than as benchmarks. The 'logit' and 'tree' findings are about factor-analytic approaches (technique plus variable selection plus time allocation), not head-to-head technique comparisons; regression sample size was n = 35 and the design was not factorial, which the authors acknowledge. The winning entry used gradient tree boosting. The profit figures rest on assumed parameters (delta = $50 incentive, CLV $500-$2,500, success rate 10-50%, base churn 1.8%) and scale with firm size. The paper predates modern ensembles, class-imbalance methods and uplift modelling, and its own discussion notes that targeting on churn risk and targeting on response to retention offers 'need not be the same'.
